submodules.title: 1. Reading Financial Statements
submodules.intro: What do a company's three main reports tell you?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: READING FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
After studying the economy and the industry, analysts zoom in on one company. Its financial statements are like a health report: they show what it owns, what it earned and where its cash went. A listed Indian company publishes three main statements. All examples here are made up, and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Listed companies in India must publish their financial results every quarter, so you can follow a company's numbers four times a year instead of waiting for one annual report.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE BALANCE SHEET
A balance sheet is a snapshot on one date. It lists:
• Assets: what the company owns, such as cash, stock, machines and buildings.
• Liabilities: what it owes, such as loans and unpaid bills.
• Equity: what is left for the owners.
The rule is: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PROFIT AND LOSS, AND CASH FLOW
• Statement of Profit and Loss: covers a period, such as a quarter or a year. Revenue minus expenses gives profit.
• Cash flow statement: tracks real cash coming in and going out, split into operating, investing and financing activities.
Profit and cash are not the same thing, so check both.

🍕 MINI CASE: A FICTIONAL BAKERY
Crumb & Co Ltd (fictional) owns ₹500 of assets and owes ₹300. Its equity is 500 - 300 = ₹200. This year it earned ₹1,000 from sales and spent ₹850 on costs, so its profit is ₹150. Whether it also collected that money in cash is a question for the cash flow statement.

🧪 TRY IT: BALANCE THE SHEET
A fictional firm has assets of ₹800 and equity of ₹350. What are its liabilities? (Answer: 800 - 350 = ₹450.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
The balance sheet shows a snapshot, the profit and loss statement shows performance over a period, and the cash flow statement shows real cash. Read all three together, because one statement never tells the whole story.

quiz.question: Which statement is a snapshot of assets and liabilities on one date?
quiz.explanation: The balance sheet shows what a company owns and owes on a particular date.

quiz.question: Which equation always holds on a balance sheet?
quiz.explanation: Everything a company owns is funded either by what it owes or by the owners' equity.

quiz.question: A firm has revenue of ₹1,000 and expenses of ₹850. What is its profit?
Which statement tracks the real cash moving in and out of a company?
quiz.explanation: The cash flow statement shows actual cash from operating, investing and financing activities.

quiz.question: Why should you read all three statements together?
options: Each shows a different side, and profit is not the same as cash
It is a legal rule for investors
quiz.explanation: Each statement answers a different question, so together they give a fuller picture.

submodules.title: 2. Annual Report Sections
submodules.intro: Where do you look inside a company's annual report?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: ANNUAL REPORT SECTIONS
An annual report is a long document that a listed company publishes every year. It is more than numbers. It also holds the management's story, the auditor's opinion and many small details. Knowing where to look saves time. All examples are fictional and this is not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Annual reports of listed Indian companies are free to read. You can usually find them on the company's website and on the NSE and BSE websites.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN SECTIONS
• Directors' report: the board's summary of the year, including performance and dividends.
• Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A): management's view of the industry, risks, opportunities and outlook.
• Corporate governance report: how the board is made up and how the company is run.
• Auditor's report: an independent professional's opinion on whether the accounts give a fair picture.
• Financial statements and notes to accounts: the numbers and the explanations behind them.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHY THE NOTES AND THE AUDITOR MATTER
The notes to accounts explain details that the main statements only summarise, such as loans, accounting policies, related-party transactions and possible future obligations. The auditor's report usually gives a clean opinion. A qualified opinion or an extra warning paragraph means the auditor found something worth reading carefully.

🍕 MINI CASE: SKIPPING TO THE BACK
Aarav opens the fictional Blue Harbour Foods Ltd report and jumps straight to the auditor's report and the notes. He finds a note about a large loan to a related company. That is not proof of a problem, but it gives him a question to research.

🧪 TRY IT: WHERE WOULD YOU LOOK?
Match each question to a section: (a) What does management expect for the industry next year? (b) Did the auditor raise any concern? (c) What are the details behind the loan figure?
(Answers: a = MD&A, b = auditor's report, c = notes to accounts.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
The annual report is a toolkit. Use the MD&A for the story, the auditor's report for independent opinion and the notes for detail, and always read management's claims with a questioning mind.

quiz.question: Which section gives management's view of the industry, risks and outlook?
quiz.explanation: The MD&A is where management discusses the business environment and outlook.

quiz.question: Who writes the auditor's report?
quiz.explanation: An independent auditor gives an opinion on whether the accounts present a fair picture.

quiz.question: Where would you find details behind a loan figure on the balance sheet?
quiz.explanation: The notes explain the numbers in more detail.

quiz.question: What does a qualified opinion in an auditor's report suggest?
options: The auditor found something worth reading carefully
quiz.explanation: A qualified opinion flags an issue and is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict by itself.

quiz.question: Where can you usually find a listed company's annual report for free?
options: Only from a broker for a fee
On the company website and exchange websites
quiz.explanation: Listed companies publish annual reports publicly, including on NSE and BSE.

submodules.title: 3. Key Ratios
submodules.intro: How do you turn raw numbers into comparable measures?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: KEY RATIOS
A big company and a small company cannot be compared by raw profit alone. A ratio divides one number by another so you can compare fairly. Ratios fall into groups, and each group answers one question about the business. All examples are fictional and not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A ₹100 crore profit sounds huge, but on ₹10,000 crore of sales it is a thin margin of 1%. The ratio tells you more than the raw number.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE FIVE FAMILIES OF RATIOS
• Profitability: how much profit does the business keep?
• Valuation: how expensive is the share relative to the business?
• Liquidity: can it pay its short-term bills?
• Leverage: how much does it rely on debt?
• Efficiency: how well does it use its assets?
The next lessons cover each family in turn.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW TO READ A RATIO
• Compare with the company's own past years to see the trend.
• Compare with similar companies in the same industry.
• Never compare firms from very different industries, because normal ratios differ by industry.
• One ratio rarely tells the full story.

🍕 MINI CASE: BIG vs SMALL
BigMart Ltd (fictional) earns ₹50 profit on ₹500 sales. Corner Cart Ltd (fictional) earns ₹5 profit on ₹50 sales. BigMart has ten times the profit, but both keep 10 paise of every rupee of sales. On this measure they are equal.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE MARGIN
Profit margin = profit ÷ sales x 100. A firm earns ₹30 profit on ₹600 sales. What is its margin? (Answer: 30 ÷ 600 x 100 = 5%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Ratios turn raw numbers into fair comparisons. Group them by the question they answer, compare them over time and against similar firms, and never rely on just one.

quiz.question: Why do analysts use ratios instead of raw numbers?
options: Ratios allow fair comparison between firms of different sizes
quiz.explanation: Dividing one number by another makes companies of different sizes comparable.

quiz.question: A firm earns ₹30 profit on ₹600 sales. What is its profit margin?
Which ratio family tells you whether a company can pay its short-term bills?
quiz.explanation: Liquidity ratios show the ability to meet short-term obligations.

quiz.question: What is a sensible way to judge a ratio?
options: Compare with past years and with similar firms
quiz.explanation: Trends and peer comparisons give a ratio meaning.

quiz.question: Why avoid comparing firms from very different industries?
options: Normal ratio levels differ across industries
Ratios do not exist for them
quiz.explanation: A normal margin or debt level in one industry may look odd in another.

submodules.title: 4. Profitability Ratios
submodules.intro: How much profit does a business really keep?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: PROFITABILITY RATIOS
Profitability ratios show how well a company turns sales and capital into profit. They help answer a simple question: is this a business that keeps a healthy share of what it earns? All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Two companies can earn the same profit, yet one may have used far more money to earn it. Return ratios reveal that difference.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MARGINS
• Operating margin = operating profit ÷ revenue x 100. It shows profit from the core business before interest and tax.
• Net profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue x 100. It shows what is left after all costs, interest and tax.
Higher margins usually mean more room to absorb shocks, but typical margins differ a lot across industries.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: ROE AND ROCE
• ROE (Return on Equity) = net profit ÷ shareholders' equity x 100. It shows profit earned on the owners' money.
• ROCE (Return on Capital Employed) = operating profit (EBIT) ÷ capital employed x 100, where capital employed is roughly total assets minus current liabilities. It shows how well all the money in the business, including debt, is used.
A high ROE built mainly on heavy debt can be risky, so look at debt as well.

🍕 MINI CASE: SAME PROFIT, DIFFERENT USE
QuickLoom Ltd and SlowLoom Ltd (both fictional) each earn ₹30 profit. QuickLoom uses ₹200 of equity, so its ROE is 15%. SlowLoom needs ₹300 of equity, so its ROE is 10%. QuickLoom uses the owners' money more effectively.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE ROE
A fictional firm earns ₹24 profit on equity of ₹300. What is its ROE? (Answer: 24 ÷ 300 x 100 = 8%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Margins show how much profit a business keeps from sales, and ROE and ROCE show how well it uses money. Compare them over several years and with similar firms, and check debt before trusting a high ROE.

quiz.question: What does net profit margin measure?
options: Net profit as a share of revenue
quiz.explanation: Net margin = net profit ÷ revenue x 100.

quiz.question: A firm earns ₹24 profit on equity of ₹300. What is its ROE?
Revenue is ₹800 and net profit is ₹80. What is the net margin?
What does ROCE look at?
options: Profit earned on all capital used, including debt
quiz.explanation: ROCE compares operating profit with the total capital employed in the business.

quiz.question: Why be careful with a very high ROE?
options: It can be built on heavy debt, which adds risk
It means no tax is paid
quiz.explanation: Debt can inflate ROE, so check the leverage behind it.

submodules.title: 5. Valuation Ratios
submodules.intro: Is a share's price high or low compared with the business?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: VALUATION RATIOS
A great company can still be a poor purchase if its price is too high, and a weak company can look cheap for a reason. Valuation ratios compare a share's price with what the business earns or owns. They are tools for asking questions, not for deciding. All examples are fictional and not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A low P/E does not always mean a bargain. Sometimes the market expects profits to fall, so the price is low for a reason.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN VALUATION RATIOS
• P/E (Price to Earnings) = share price ÷ earnings per share (EPS). It shows how many rupees the market pays for each rupee of yearly profit.
• P/B (Price to Book) = share price ÷ book value per share. It compares the price with the company's net assets.
• EV/EBITDA = enterprise value ÷ EBITDA. It values the whole business, including debt, against operating earnings.
• PEG = P/E ÷ expected yearly profit growth rate. It adjusts P/E for growth.
• Dividend yield = dividend per share ÷ share price x 100.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: USING THEM WISELY
• Compare a ratio with the same company's past and with similar firms.
• Fast-growing firms often have higher P/E ratios.
• Banks are often judged using P/B because their assets are mostly financial.
• Profits can be unusual in one year, which distorts P/E.

🍕 MINI CASE: SAME PRICE, DIFFERENT STORY
Two fictional firms each trade at ₹150 per share. GrowFast Ltd has EPS of ₹5, so its P/E is 30. SteadyBrew Ltd has EPS of ₹15, so its P/E is 10. The market pays more per rupee of profit for GrowFast, probably because it expects faster growth. That expectation may or may not come true.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE P/E
A fictional share costs ₹150 and EPS is ₹6. What is the P/E? (Answer: 150 ÷ 6 = 25.) A share paying ₹4 dividend at a price of ₹100 has a dividend yield of 4%.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Valuation ratios compare price with earnings, assets and growth. Use them alongside business quality, compare within the same industry, and remember that a cheap-looking ratio is a question, not a signal to buy.

quiz.question: How is P/E calculated?
quiz.explanation: P/E = share price ÷ EPS.

quiz.question: A share costs ₹150 and EPS is ₹6. What is the P/E?
A share pays a ₹5 dividend and costs ₹100. What is the dividend yield?
What does a low P/E always mean?
options: The share is always a bargain
Nothing certain; it may reflect expected weak profits
quiz.explanation: A low P/E can be a bargain or a warning, so it needs investigation.

quiz.question: Which ratio compares a share's price with the company's net assets per share?
quiz.explanation: P/B compares price with book value per share.

submodules.title: 6. Liquidity and Leverage
submodules.intro: Can the company pay its bills, and how much does it owe?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: LIQUIDITY AND LEVERAGE
A company can be profitable and still get into trouble if it cannot pay its bills on time or if it owes too much. Liquidity looks at short-term bills. Leverage looks at how much a company relies on borrowed money. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Debt is not always bad. Many healthy companies borrow to grow. The danger is borrowing more than the business can comfortably repay.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: LIQUIDITY
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities.
• Current assets: cash, stock and money to be received within a year.
• Current liabilities: bills and loans due within a year.
A ratio above 1 means current assets cover current bills. A ratio well below 1 can signal stress, though some businesses normally run low ratios.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: LEVERAGE
• Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity. It shows how much debt there is for every rupee of the owners' money.
• Interest coverage = operating profit (EBIT) ÷ interest expense. It shows how many times profit covers the interest bill.
A higher coverage is safer. Very low coverage means a small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay.
Debt-to-equity is not used the same way for banks, whose business is to borrow and lend.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO BUILDERS
SolidBase Builders Ltd (fictional) has debt of ₹100 and equity of ₹200, so its debt-to-equity is 0.5. HighRise Homes Ltd (fictional) has debt of ₹400 and equity of ₹200, so its debt-to-equity is 2. If interest rates rise or sales slow, HighRise has less room to manage.

🧪 TRY IT: CURRENT RATIO AND COVERAGE
A firm has current assets of ₹240 and current liabilities of ₹300. Current ratio = 240 ÷ 300 = 0.8. Another firm has EBIT of ₹90 and interest of ₹30. Coverage = 90 ÷ 30 = 3 times.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Liquidity checks short-term safety and leverage checks long-term debt strain. Look at the trend and compare with similar firms, because normal levels differ by industry.

quiz.question: How is the current ratio calculated?
quiz.explanation: The current ratio compares short-term assets with short-term liabilities.

quiz.question: Current assets are ₹240 and current liabilities are ₹300. What is the current ratio?
Debt is ₹400 and equity is ₹200. What is the debt-to-equity ratio?
EBIT is ₹90 and interest expense is ₹30. What is the interest coverage?
What does very low interest coverage suggest?
options: A small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay
The company is certain to grow
quiz.explanation: Low coverage means little cushion between profit and the interest bill.

submodules.title: 7. Efficiency Ratios
submodules.intro: How well does a company use what it owns?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: EFFICIENCY RATIOS
Efficiency ratios ask how well a company turns its assets, stock and customer bills into sales and cash. A company that wastes assets or waits too long for payment can look healthy on paper while cash gets stuck. All examples are fictional and not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A business that collects money from customers faster can run on less borrowed money, even without selling anything extra.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN EFFICIENCY RATIOS
• Asset turnover = revenue ÷ total assets. It shows how many rupees of sales each rupee of assets creates.
• Inventory days = inventory ÷ cost of goods sold x 365. It shows how long stock sits before it is sold.
• Receivable days = receivables ÷ revenue x 365. It shows how long customers take to pay.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOW TO READ THEM
• Rising inventory days can mean slow sales or too much stock.
• Rising receivable days can mean customers are paying late.
• Normal levels differ a lot by industry. A grocery chain turns stock quickly, while a heavy machinery maker holds stock longer.
• Watch the trend over several years.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE SLOW PAYER
SteadyCloth Ltd (fictional) sells ₹730 of cloth a year, and customers owe it ₹60. Receivable days = 60 ÷ 730 x 365 = 30 days. Next year receivables rise to ₹120 on the same sales, which is 60 days. Profit may look unchanged, but the company is waiting twice as long for its cash.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE DAYS
A fictional firm has revenue of ₹1,095 and receivables of ₹90. Receivable days = 90 ÷ 1,095 x 365 = 30 days. Another has revenue of ₹1,000 and assets of ₹500. Asset turnover = 2.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Efficiency ratios show how quickly a business turns assets into sales and sales into cash. Rising stock days or customer-payment days are worth investigating, but compare them with similar firms.

quiz.question: What does asset turnover measure?
options: Sales created per rupee of assets
quiz.explanation: Asset turnover = revenue ÷ total assets.

quiz.question: Revenue is ₹1,000 and total assets are ₹500. What is the asset turnover?
What do receivable days show?
options: How long customers take to pay
quiz.explanation: Receivable days measure the average time to collect money from customers.

quiz.question: Receivables are ₹90 and revenue is ₹1,095. What are the receivable days?
What can rising inventory days suggest?
options: Slow sales or too much stock
quiz.explanation: Stock staying longer before sale can mean weak demand or over-stocking.

submodules.title: 8. Qualitative Factors
submodules.intro: What matters about a company that numbers cannot show?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: QUALITATIVE FACTORS
Numbers describe the past, but they cannot fully show the quality of people and the strength of a business. Qualitative factors are the things you judge by reading and thinking rather than by calculating. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Investor Warren Buffett popularised the idea of an 'economic moat', a lasting advantage that protects a business from competitors, like a moat around a castle.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PEOPLE AND GOVERNANCE
• Management: look at their track record, how they treat shareholders and whether they explain their results honestly.
• Promoter holding: promoters are the founders or controlling owners. A meaningful holding can mean their interests line up with other shareholders, but the quality of the promoters matters more than the percentage.
• Governance: an independent board, clear disclosures and fair dealing with related parties.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MOAT AND BRAND
A moat can come from:
• A trusted brand that customers choose again and again.
• Low costs that rivals cannot match.
• Switching costs, where customers find it hard to leave.
• Licences or technology that others cannot easily copy.
A moat is never permanent. New technology or rules can weaken it.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO TOOTHPASTE MAKERS
MintFresh Ltd (fictional) has a brand families have trusted for decades, so shops stock it and buyers pick it without thinking. NewFoam Ltd (fictional) has a similar product but no loyal base and spends heavily to attract customers. MintFresh appears to have a stronger moat. Whether that is already reflected in its price is a separate question.

🧪 TRY IT: SPOT THE MOAT
Which is more likely to be a moat: (a) a brand customers trust and reuse, or (b) a bright office building? (Answer: a.) Pick a company you know and write down one possible moat and one way it could weaken.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Good numbers need good people and a durable advantage behind them. Study management, governance and the moat, but remember these judgments are opinions and can be wrong.

quiz.question: What is an economic moat?
options: A lasting advantage that protects a business from rivals
quiz.explanation: A moat is a durable competitive advantage.

quiz.question: Who are promoters?
options: The founders or controlling owners of a company
quiz.explanation: Promoters are the people or groups who founded or control the company.

quiz.question: Which of these could be a source of a moat?
options: A long list of awards only
quiz.explanation: A trusted brand that drives repeat buying is a common moat.

quiz.question: Is a moat permanent?
options: Yes, if the company is old
Yes, if the P/E is low
No, new technology or rules can weaken it
quiz.explanation: Advantages can erode over time, so they need to be rechecked.

quiz.question: Why are qualitative judgments risky to rely on alone?
options: They are opinions and can be wrong
quiz.explanation: They involve judgment, so they work best alongside numbers and evidence.

submodules.title: 9. Shareholding Patterns
submodules.intro: Who owns a company, and why does it matter?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: SHAREHOLDING PATTERNS
A company's shareholding pattern shows who owns its shares. Listed companies in India report it to the exchanges every quarter, so you can see how ownership changes over time. Changes can raise useful questions, though they are never proof of what will happen. All examples are fictional and not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Shareholding patterns are filed quarterly with the exchanges and are free to view, so anyone can see whether big investors are buying or selling over time.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHO THE OWNERS ARE
• Promoters: founders or controlling owners.
• FPIs (Foreign Portfolio Investors, often still called FIIs): overseas funds and investors.
• DIIs (Domestic Institutional Investors): Indian institutions such as mutual funds and insurance companies.
• Public: everyone else, including small retail investors.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PLEDGED SHARES
Sometimes promoters borrow money by pledging some of their shares to a lender as security. If the share price falls a lot, the lender may be able to sell those shares, which can add pressure on the price. A high pledged share of the promoters' holding is therefore a risk to examine.
Pledged % = pledged shares ÷ promoters' shares x 100.

🍕 MINI CASE: READING THE TABLE
Over four quarters, the fictional Kaveri Cement Ltd shows promoters steady at 55%, mutual funds rising from 8% to 12%, and foreign investors easing from 20% to 17%. This does not tell Aarav what to do. It gives him questions: why are domestic funds adding and foreign funds trimming?

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE PLEDGE
Promoters hold 5 crore shares and have pledged 2 crore. Pledged % = 2 ÷ 5 x 100 = 40%. Now try: promoters hold 8 crore and pledged 2 crore. What is the pledged %? (Answer: 25%.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Shareholding patterns show who owns a company and how that is changing. Watch promoter pledges and big shifts by institutions, and treat them as clues to research, not instructions.

quiz.question: How often do listed companies report their shareholding pattern to the exchanges?
options: Only when asked by a friend
quiz.explanation: Shareholding patterns are filed quarterly.

quiz.question: Which group includes mutual funds and insurance companies?
quiz.explanation: Domestic institutional investors include Indian mutual funds and insurers.

quiz.question: What are pledged shares?
options: Shares offered to a lender as security for a loan
quiz.explanation: Pledging means using shares as security to borrow money.

quiz.question: Promoters hold 5 crore shares and have pledged 2 crore. What is the pledged percentage?
Why can a high pledged share be a risk?
options: The lender may sell shares if the price falls a lot, adding pressure
It means the company is government-owned
quiz.explanation: Forced selling by lenders can push the price down further.

submodules.title: 10. Red Flags
submodules.intro: Which warning signs should make you look more closely?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: RED FLAGS
A red flag is a warning sign that makes you look harder at a company. It is not proof of wrongdoing. Many healthy companies show one now and then. The danger is several flags together, or flags that keep repeating. All examples are fictional and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Most accounting problems that surprise investors left clues earlier, often in the notes to accounts or in the gap between profit and cash.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WARNING SIGNS IN THE NUMBERS
• Debt rising much faster than profit or sales.
• Profit rising while operating cash flow keeps falling.
• Receivable days or inventory days climbing for several periods.
• Interest coverage shrinking toward 1.
• A high share of promoter shares pledged.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WARNING SIGNS IN THE PEOPLE AND PAPERWORK
• Auditors resigning or being changed often, or a qualified audit opinion.
• Large related-party transactions, where the company deals with firms linked to its promoters.
• Frequent changes in accounting methods.
• Top managers leaving suddenly and repeatedly.
• Vague explanations from management when asked about results.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO DO WITH A FLAG
Write the flag down, look for an explanation in the annual report, see whether it repeats over several years and compare with similar firms. Treat it as a question, not a verdict.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE QUIET GAP
BrightLine Textiles Ltd (fictional) reports profit rising from ₹100 to ₹150 over three years, but operating cash flow falls from ₹110 to ₹30. Receivable days have doubled. Meera notes this as a flag and researches why customers are paying so slowly.

🧪 TRY IT: FLAG OR NOT?
Which is a stronger reason to investigate: (a) a firm opens one new office, or (b) a firm's profit rises for three years while its cash flow falls every year? (Answer: b.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Red flags are signals to research, not proof. Look for patterns across numbers, people and paperwork, and be most careful when several flags appear together.

quiz.question: What is a red flag in company analysis?
options: A warning sign that deserves a closer look
quiz.explanation: A red flag is a prompt to investigate, not proof of wrongdoing.

quiz.question: Which combination is a stronger warning sign?
options: Profit and cash flow both rising
Profit rising for years while operating cash flow keeps falling
quiz.explanation: A growing gap between profit and cash is worth investigating.

quiz.question: Why can frequent auditor changes be a concern?
options: They can signal disagreements or problems worth checking
quiz.explanation: Repeated changes can hint at issues, so they deserve a closer look.

quiz.question: What are related-party transactions?
options: Deals between the company and firms linked to its promoters or directors
quiz.explanation: They are dealings with linked parties, which need fair terms and clear disclosure.

quiz.question: What is a sensible response to a red flag?
options: Check the explanation, see if it repeats and compare with peers
quiz.explanation: Treat a flag as a question to research before reaching any conclusion.

submodules.title: 11. Cash Flow and Earnings Quality
submodules.intro: Is a company's profit backed by real cash?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: CASH FLOW AND EARNINGS QUALITY
A company can show a profit on paper and still run short of cash. That is why analysts compare profit with the actual cash coming in. 'Earnings quality' means how well reported profit is backed by real cash. All companies here are fictional, and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A company can be profitable and still fail if customers pay late and it runs out of cash to pay its own bills.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE THREE CASH FLOWS
• Operating cash flow (CFO): cash from the core business.
• Investing cash flow: cash spent on or earned from assets such as machinery and property.
• Financing cash flow: cash from loans, share issues, repayments and dividends.
Healthy firms usually show positive operating cash flow over the years.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: FREE CASH FLOW
Free cash flow (FCF) = operating cash flow - capital expenditure (money spent on machines, factories and similar assets). It shows the cash left after the business has paid to keep and grow itself.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: PROFIT vs CASH
If profit keeps rising but operating cash flow keeps falling, ask why. Sales may be made on credit that customers have not paid yet, or stock may be piling up. One year proves little, so look at several years.

🍕 MINI CASE: TWO FICTIONAL FIRMS
Steady Steel Ltd reports ₹100 profit and ₹110 operating cash flow. Its profit is backed by cash.
PaperTrail Traders Ltd reports ₹100 profit but only ₹20 operating cash flow, because customers have not paid. That gap is a question to investigate, not proof of a problem.

🧪 TRY IT: FREE CASH FLOW
A fictional firm has operating cash flow of ₹500 and spends ₹200 on new machines. FCF = 500 - 200 = ₹300.
Now try: operating cash flow ₹80 and capital expenditure ₹50. What is the FCF? (Answer: ₹30.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Profit is an opinion backed by accounting rules, and cash is a fact. Compare the two over several years, and treat large gaps as questions to research.

quiz.question: What does operating cash flow show?
options: Cash from the company's core business
quiz.explanation: Operating cash flow shows cash generated by the main business activities.

quiz.question: How is free cash flow calculated?
quiz.explanation: FCF is the cash left after spending on assets needed to run and grow the business.

quiz.question: Operating cash flow is ₹80 and capital expenditure is ₹50. What is the FCF?
Profit keeps rising but operating cash flow keeps falling. What should you do?
quiz.explanation: A growing gap may come from unpaid customer bills or piling stock, so it is worth checking.

quiz.question: Why look at several years of cash flow instead of one?
options: One year can be unusual and prove little
quiz.explanation: A single year can be distorted by one-off events, so a longer view is more reliable.

submodules.title: 12. Company Analysis Checklist
submodules.intro: How do you put all the company clues together?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE COMPANY CHECKLIST
You have studied statements, ratios, cash flow, management and red flags. This capstone puts them into one reusable checklist. The goal is to ask better questions, not to predict prices. All examples are fictional, and this is education, not advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Professional analysts rarely trust one ratio. They build a picture from many clues and stay ready to change their mind.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE CHECKLIST
1. Business: what does it sell, and who buys it?
2. Growth: are sales and profit rising over several years?
3. Profitability: are margins, ROE and ROCE healthy compared with similar firms?
4. Cash: is profit backed by operating cash flow?
5. Debt: is debt manageable, and is interest comfortably covered?
6. Valuation: is the price reasonable compared with earnings and with peers?
7. People: how do management, governance and shareholding look?
8. Red flags: anything unusual in the annual report or auditor notes?

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON TRAPS
• Judging by one ratio alone.
• Comparing firms from very different industries.
• Trusting a cheap-looking P/E without asking why it is low.
• Forgetting that past results do not guarantee the future.

🍕 MINI CASE: FILLING THE CHECKLIST
Meera studies the fictional Gaon Grains Ltd. She notes steady sales growth, moderate debt and cash flow that follows profit. She also notes a high valuation and a recent auditor change. She ends with a list of questions to research, not a prediction.

🧪 TRY IT: YOUR OWN CHECKLIST
Pick a well-known company and fill each of the eight checklist points in one line using its public annual report. Finish with three questions you still cannot answer. Discuss it with a parent, teacher or guardian.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Combine business, numbers, cash, people and red flags into one picture, and list what is still unknown. No checklist guarantees returns. Involve a parent or guardian in any real money decision.

quiz.question: What is the main goal of the company checklist?
options: To ask better questions about a company
quiz.explanation: The checklist builds a fuller picture and highlights open questions.

quiz.question: Which item belongs on the checklist?
options: Whether profit is backed by operating cash flow
quiz.explanation: Checking that profit is backed by cash is a core part of company analysis.

quiz.question: Which is a common trap?
options: Judging a company by one ratio alone
quiz.explanation: One ratio rarely tells the full story.

quiz.question: Why is comparing firms from very different industries risky?
options: Their ratios often mean different things
quiz.explanation: Normal margins and debt levels differ a lot between industries.

quiz.question: Does any checklist guarantee returns?
quiz.explanation: No method guarantees returns, so involve a parent or guardian in real money decisions.
